body:
`run_with_heartbeat` (`template/src/pdca_harness/progress.py:25`) waits on the direct child and returns. Nothing ever looks at what that child *spawned*: on a normal exit, any process the command left behind — a backgrounded test, a server a test forgot to stop, a build tree whose leader died — simply survives. Under `shell=True` (every gate) the direct child is only a shell, so the surviving work is the rule, not the edge case.

The instance-staged timeout work (#368 / instance #187) sweeps the process group, but only on the **timeout and interrupt paths**, and only for a *bounded* child (`start_new_session=timeout is not None`). A child that exits normally — the overwhelmingly common case — leaves its group unswept, and an unbounded child (the headless model leaves pass no timeout) is not even sessionized, so its stragglers cannot be swept at all.

## Measured

On the instance host, 2026-07-31:

```
PID 2775549  started Jul 30 19:54:10  elapsed 21:04:39  cpu 21:03:01
.../wyrd.pdca-wt/target/debug/deps/multipart_protocol-4f1e4f851285d1d0
    an_owned_entry_that_cannot_fit_one_batch_is_named_not_committed --exact --nocapture
```

A single test process, reparented to the user manager, burning ~100% of a core for 21 hours. Its test function exists in **no current tree** — it came from a *prior cycle's* patched tree; the lane worktree was reset and rebuilt underneath it for the next bundles while it spun on.

The CPU burn is the visible cost. The worse one is cross-cycle interference: a straggler from cycle N still holds its ports, file locks and fixtures when cycle N+1's gates run in the same lane worktree — the class of one-off, never-reproducible gate failure measured in #371 (`issue_648`: a gating `cargo test` red within ~90s, green on every re-run).

## Suggested shape

- Sessionize every child whose stdio the harness owns: `start_new_session = capture or stream_json or timeout is not None`. A captured gate and a streamed headless leaf hold no tty, so a new session is safe; the interactive leaves (no capture, no stream, no bound) keep the terminal exactly as today.
- After the normal `proc.wait()` returns, probe the group (`os.killpg(pgid, 0)`): if members survive the leader, SIGTERM → short grace → SIGKILL, with one stderr note naming the swept command — the straggler is also a *signal* (a test or leaf that leaks processes), so it should be visible, not silent.
- Widen the existing Ctrl-C/abort sweep condition from "bounded" to "sessionized", so an interrupted captured child is swept too.

`_kill_tree` from the #368 staging already resolves the group id and escalates correctly; the normal-exit sweep can share it.

A rendered instance (getwyrd/wyrd-pdca) is staging this locally, pending upstream.

comments.body: Implementation trap found while staging this in the instance: the normal-exit sweep must run **before** the capture streams close, mirroring the timeout path's kill-then-close order. A straggler inheriting the capture pipe keeps the drain thread blocked past its join timeout, and closing a file another thread is mid-read on waits for that reader — sweep-after-close deadlocks the call until the straggler exits of its own accord (measured: two ~5-minute hangs in the test suite before the reorder). Also needs a POSIX guard: `killpg`/`setsid` don't exist on Windows, so sessionization and the sweep are gated on `os.name == "posix"` there, keeping pre-existing behaviour.

Second implementation note from the instance staging's PR review: on hosts where PID 1 does not reap adopted children (minimal-container inits), the group signal turns an orphaned straggler into a **zombie** rather than removing it — the CPU/ports/locks are released at kill, but the process-table entry accumulates, and `kill(pid, 0)`-style liveness probes (including the harness's own tests) read the zombie as alive. This equally affects the pre-existing timeout kill path, so it is a property of the kill strategy overall, not of the normal-exit sweep alone.

The clean shape is a **subreaper**: the process that owns the session takes `PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER` and `waitpid()`s the descendants it adopts. One hazard to design around: a naive `waitpid(-1)` reaper thread in the driver can steal exit statuses from concurrent `Popen.wait()`s (the driver runs lanes concurrently), and CPython treats ECHILD in `_try_wait` as a clean exit — corrupting a gate verdict is strictly worse than a zombie row in `ps`. So the reaper needs its own scope: either an intermediate supervisor process per sessionized child, or a pid-registry that restricts what the driver may reap. Deferred from the instance staging for exactly that reason; belongs in the engine-native design here.

title: progress: a finished child's stragglers are never swept — a leaked test process from a prior cycle burned a core for 21 hours
